S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder is characterized by intrusive, unwanted obsessions and repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce distress or prevent feared outcomes, with the cycle becoming time-consuming or functionally impairing. It is distinguished from ordinary worry or perfectionism by the ego-dystonic quality of the thoughts and the clearly excessive or unrealistic nature of the compulsive responses; its course is often gradual, with worsening during stress or life transitions.

patient.stressor_event: Death of a close family member
patient.stressor: Tanika Mcadory’s symptoms became more visible after the death of a beloved aunt who had been a gospel singer and a steady supporter of her community art projects. While preparing a small memorial installation, Tanika found that intrusive, unwanted thoughts about getting the tribute wrong began driving repetitive reviewing and arranging rituals that went beyond her usual careful studio process. She remained able to complete most obligations, but the extra time and distress caused her to miss one grant deadline and withdraw from a low-key gallery talk she had been looking forward to. Recognizing that the pattern was no longer just artistic precision, she used her artist guild’s referral network to schedule an evaluation with a psychiatrist.

S065.manifestation: I came in because when I was working on my aunt’s memorial piece, I kept getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow—like one wrong photo placement or color choice would mean I didn’t love her enough—and I couldn’t just brush them off like normal creative doubts.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: I’ll end up rereading the label text, nudging the same objects on the table, and checking the layout photos over and over until it feels ‘settled,’ even though part of me knows it’s already fine and I’m just losing studio time.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: I’m still getting most of my work done, but the extra time I lose in the studio already cost me a grant deadline and made me back out of a gallery talk I had actually wanted to do.
